newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bond ylds end up, nothing new from RBA.
newsitem.headline: Australian bond ylds end up, nothing new from RBA.

text.p: *Australian bond yields ended higher reflecting weakness in U.S. Treasuries in Asian trading and after the RBA August bulletin ran on similar lines to Governor's speech last week.

Australian bond yields ended with a firmer bias reflecting weakness in U.S. Treasuries in Asian trading and after the Reserve Bank's August bulletin ran on similar lines to Governor Ian Macfarlane's speech last week.

A misinterpreted reading of the report by one wire service suggesting monetary policy could be eased to provide further support for growth, when in fact the report referred to past easings in policy, sent short-dated futures up smartly.
However, the December bill futures contract later ended unchanged at 95.24 after touching a high of 95.30.
"The RBA's Quarterly Report is certainly bullish on the Australian economy, but not nearly as bullish as the first market interpretation," said HSBC analysts in a report.
The RBA said present policy settings have scope to accommodate higher growth, while domestic sourced inflation appears to be in check and that wage pressures have eased in recent months.
The RBA added that while growth is more likely to accelerate than slow down, second quarter demand and output expansion is likely to be at a slower pace than the first quarter.
"Overall the report confirms that the RBA governor Ian Macfarlane is determined to be cheerful about the economy," the HSBC Markets report said.

"After five rate cuts leaving us with the lowest interest rates in nearly thirty years, he is evidently convinced that what we need now is optimism and confidence in the Australian economy in the year ahead," it added.

However, the market is yet to be convinced that another interest rate cut is not on the cards with the December contract still discounting a 25 basis point easing in the 5.0 percent official cash interest rate.

The local market showed a mild outperforming bias against the U.S., reversing some of the spread widening seen late on Monday. New Zealand debt was once again under pressure as the fragility of the N.Z. dollar continued to weigh on the market.
